abstract:
While adversarial training has been extensively studied for ResNet architectures and low resolution datasets like CIFAR-10, much less is known for ImageNet. Given the recent debate about whether transformers are more robust than convnets, we revisit adversarial training on ImageNet comparing ViTs and ConvNeXts. Extensive experiments show that minor changes in architecture, most notably replacing PatchStem with ConvStem, and training scheme have a significant impact on the achieved robustness. These changes not only increase robustness in the seen $\ell_\infty$-threat model, but even more so improve generalization to unseen $\ell_1/\ell_2$-attacks. 
Our modified ConvNeXt, ConvNeXt + ConvStem, yields the most robust $\ell_\infty$-models across different ranges of model parameters and FLOPs, while our ViT + ConvStem yields the best generalization to unseen threat models.

# Revisiting Adversarial Training for ImageNet: Architectures, Training and Generalization across Threat Models Naman D Singh*12 Francesco Croce*12 Matthias Hein12 # Abstract While adversarial training has been extensively studied for ResNet architectures and low resolution datasets like CIFAR-10, much less is known for ImageNet. Given the recent debate about whether transformers are more robust than convnets, we revisit adversarial training on ImageNet comparing ViTs and ConvNeXts. Extensive experiments show that minor changes in architecture, most notably replacing PatchStem with ConvStem, and training scheme have a significant impact on the achieved robustness. These changes not only increase robustness in the seen $\ell_{\infty}$ -threat model, but even more so improve generalization to unseen $\ell_1 / \ell_2$ -robustness. Our modified ConvNeXt, ConvNeXt + ConvStem, yields the most robust models across different ranges of model parameters and FLOPs. # 1. Introduction Adversarial training (Madry et al., 2018) is the standard technique to obtain classifiers robust against adversarial perturbations. Many works have extensively analyzed several aspects of adversarial training, leading to further improvements. These include changes in the training scheme, i.e. using different loss functions (Zhang et al., 2019; Rade & Moosavi-Dezfooli, 2022; Pang et al., 2022), tuning hyperparameters like learning rate schedule or weight decay, increasing the strength of the attack at training time, adding label smoothing and stochastic weight averaging (Gowal et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2021). Also, complementing the training set with pseudo-labelled (Carmon et al., 2019) or synthetic (Gowal et al., 2021) data, and via specific augmentations (Rebuffi et al., 2021) yields more robust classifiers. However, these works focus on small datasets like CIFAR-10 with low resolution images, and models using variants * Equal contribution ${}^{1}$ University of Tübingen ${}^{2}$ Tübingen AI Center. AutoAttack $\ell_{\infty}$ -Robust accuracy ( $\epsilon = 4/255$ ) on ImageNet across different architectures and training schemes at resolution $224 \times 224$ . With our training scheme and replacing PatchStem with ConvStem for the ConvNeXt and ViT we outperform over a range of parameters/FLOPs existing models in terms of $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy e.g. our ConvNext-T-CvStem with 28.6M parameters achieves $49.5\%$ robust accuracy, a $5.1\%$ higher robust accuracy than the ConvNeXt-T of Debenedetti et al. (2023). of ResNet (He et al., 2016) as architecture. When considering a more challenging dataset like ImageNet, the space of possible design choices regarding model, training and evaluation protocols becomes much richer, and little work exists exploring this domain. For example, it has been recently shown that architectures like vision transformers (ViTs) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Touvron et al., 2021), mixers (Tolstikhin et al., 2021; Trockman & Kolter, 2022) and hybrids borrowing elements of different families of networks (El-Nouby et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022) are competitive or outperform convolutional networks on ImageNet, while they hardly work on e.g. CIFAR-10. In turn, ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) has been proposed as modern version of ResNet which closes the gap to transformer architectures. In this work we study the influence of architecture and training schemes on the robustness of classifiers to seen and unseen attacks. We focus on two extreme ends of architectures used on ImageNet: ViT and ConvNeXt (isotropic vs non-isotropic, attention only vs convolution only, stem with large vs small patches) and study Isotropic ConvNeXt as an intermediate architecture. We focus on training of ImageNet models robust with respect to the $\ell_{\infty}$ -threat model (i.e. perturbations have bounded $\ell_{\infty}$ -norm), but additionally track the robustness to unseen types of attacks like $\ell_2$ -bounded ones. This can reveal architectural components which lead to better generalization of robustness, which is a desirable property since typically adversarially trained models are still vulnerable to attacks not seen at training time (Kang et al., 2019). In particular, we show via extensive experiments that - using a convolutional stem instead of a patch stem leads to consistent gains in $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness and a quite large boost in the unseen $\ell_{1}$ - and $\ell_{2}$ -threat models. - using SOTA pre-trained clean models as initialization allows us to train using heavy augmentations, in contrast to what has been suggested by prior work (Bai et al., 2021; Debenedetti et al., 2023). - increasing resolution at test time leads for the $\ell_{\infty}$ -threat model with fixed radius to a stronger attack. Nevertheless, we show that increasing resolution at test time, yields improvements in $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy. Combining our various improvements we obtain state-of-the-art $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy for perturbation size $\epsilon_{\infty} = \frac{4}{255}$ at resolution $224 \times 224$ on ImageNet, see Fig. 1. We obtain $49.5\%$ robust accuracy for small and $56.1\%$ robust accuracy for large models, improving by $5.1\%$ and $2.6\%$ respectively. Furthermore, we improve SOTA when fine-tuning these models to a larger radius $\epsilon_{\infty} = 8/255$ and to other datasets. # 2. Background and Related Work Madry et al. (2018) formulated adversarial training (AT) for a classifier $f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ as the optimization problem $$ \min _ {\theta} \sum_ {(x _ {i}, y _ {i}) \in \mathcal {D}} \max _ {\delta : \| \delta \| _ {p} \leq \epsilon_ {p}} \mathcal {L} (f _ {\theta} (x _ {i} + \delta), y _ {i}) \tag {1} $$ where $\theta$ are the parameters of the classifier $f_{\theta}$ . The goal is that $f_{\theta}$ is robust against $\ell_p$ -bounded perturbations, that is the classifier should have the same prediction on $B_{p}(x_{i},\epsilon_{p})$ . In practice, the inner maximization is approximately solved with projected gradient descent (PGD), $\theta$ is optimized with SGD (or its variants) on the training set $\mathcal{D}$ , and cross-entropy loss is used as objective function $\mathcal{L}$ . AT has been shown to be an effective defense against adversarial perturbations. Many follow-up works have modified the original algorithm to further improve the robustness of the resulting models (Zhang et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020; Gowal et al., 2021; Rade & Moosavi-Dezfooli, 2022; Pang et al., 2022). The most popular threat models are $\ell_{\infty}$ - and $\ell_2$ -bounded perturbations. Several other attacks have been explored, including $\ell_1$ - or $\ell_0$ -bounded, adversarial patches, or those defined by neural perceptual metrics like LPIPS (Laidlaw et al., 2021). A problem is that models trained to be robust with respect to one threat model need not be robust with respect to unseen ones (Kang et al., 2019). Multiple-norm adversarial training (Tramér & Boneh, 2019) aims to overcome this but degrades the performance compared to adversarial training in each individual threat model. Training recipe. Gowal et al. (2020); Pang et al. (2021) analyzed in detail the influence of several fine-grained choices of training hyperparameters (batch size, weight decay, learning rate schedule, etc.) on the achieved robustness. Hendrycks et al. (2019); Chen et al. (2020) suggest to use a standard classifier pre-trained either on a larger dataset or with a self-supervised task as initialization for adversarial training for improved robustness. However, all these works focus on CIFAR-10 or other datasets with low resolution images. For ImageNet, Bai et al. (2021) argued that ViTs and ResNets attain similar robustness for several threat models if training scheme and architecture size for both is similar, while Debenedetti et al. (2023) proposed a recipe for training $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust transformers, in particular XCiT (El-Nouby et al., 2021): basic augmentation, warm-up for the radius $\epsilon_p$ and large weight decay. In contrast, (Rebuffi et al., 2022) use the standard training scheme for a large ViT-B for 300 epochs and obtain the most $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust model on ImageNet. Architectural design choices. Searching for more robust networks Wu et al. (2021); Huang et al. (2021) studied the effect of architecture design choices in ResNets, e.g. width and depth, on adversarial robustness for CIFAR-10. Recently, Peng et al. (2023) did a similar exploration on ImageNet. Tang et al. (2022) compared the robustness to seen and unseen attacks of several modern architectures on CIFAR-10 and ImageNette, and conclude that ViTs lead to better robust generalization. Finally, Xie et al. (2020) found that using smooth activation functions like GELU (Hendrycks & Gimpel, 2016) improves the robustness of adversarially trained models on ImageNet, later confirmed for CIFAR-10 as well (Gowal et al., 2020; Pang et al., 2021). Modern architectures. Since Dosovitskiy et al. (2021) showed that transformer-based architectures can be successfully used for vision tasks, a large number of works have introduced modifications of vision transformers (Touvron et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2022) achieving SOTA classification accuracy on ImageNet, outperforming ResNets and variants. In turn, several works proposed variants of training scheme and architectures to make convolutional networks competitive with ViTs (Tan & Le, 2021; Wightman et al., 2021), in particular leading to the ConvNeXt architecture of Liu et al. (2022). Moreover, hybrid models combine typical elements of ViTs and CNNs, trying to merge the strengths of the two families (El-Nouby et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2022). While these modern architectures perform similarly well on vision tasks, it is open how they differ regarding adversarial robustness. Fu et al. (2022); Gu et al. (2022) compared the robustness of normally trained ViTs and ResNets to $\ell_p$ - and patch attacks concluding that the ranking depends on the threat model. Table 1. # 3. Influence of Architecture on Adversarial Robustness to Seen and Unseen Attacks In this section we analyze existing architectures and their components regarding adversarial robustness on ImageNet. In particular, we are interested in studying which elements are beneficial for adversarial robustness $(i)$ in the threat model seen at training time and $(ii)$ to unseen attacks. Since it is the most popular and well-studied setup, we focus on adversarial training w.r.t. $\ell_{\infty}$ , and use $\ell_2$ - and $\ell_1$ -bounded attacks to measure the generalization of robustness to unseen threat models. In the first part of the section we analyze the transition from ResNet to ConvNeXt and then study in more detail ConvNeXt and ViT as two extremes of current architectures. In the second part we show that replacing the PatchStem, common to ConvNeXt as well as the ViT, with the ConvStem improves robustness in particular regarding generalization to unseen threat models. # 3.1. Experimental Setup Training setup. If not stated otherwise, we always use adversarial training (Madry et al., 2018) w.r.t. $\ell_{\infty}$ with perturbation bound $\epsilon = 4 / 255$ and 2 steps APGD (Croce & Hein, 2020b) for the inner optimization on ImageNet-1k using resolution $224\times 224$ . Note that we use the $\ell_{2}$ - or $\ell_{1}$ -threat model just for evaluation, we never do adversarial training for them. We use a cosine decaying learning rate preceded by linear warm-up. In this section, we use a basic training setting, that is only random crop as basic augmentation and 50 epochs of adversarial training initialized with a clean model obtained with standard training for 100 epochs with same setup. More details are available in App. A. In Sec. 4 we will examine the influence of other training schemes. Evaluation setup. For all experiments in the paper, un- less specified otherwise, we evaluate the robustness using AutoAttack (Croce & Hein, 2020b), which combines APGD for cross-entropy and targeted DLR loss, FAB-attack (Croce & Hein, 2020a) and the black-box Square Attack (Andriushchenko et al., 2020), on the 5000 images of the ImageNet validation set selected by RobustBench (Croce et al., 2021) at resolution $224 \times 224$ . The evaluations are done at the following radii: $\epsilon_{\infty} = 4 / 255$ , $\epsilon_{2} = 2$ , and $\epsilon_{1} = 75$ . For some marked experiments which involve a large number of evaluations we use $\mathrm{APGD}_{\mathrm{T - DLR}}$ (40 iterations, 3 restarts) which is roughly off by $1 - 2\%$ compared to full AutoAttack. # 3.2. Step-by-step Architecture Exploration Noting that ConvNeXt achieves higher robustness than a ResNet, we aim at identifying the key steps of Liu et al. (2022) in their transformation from a ResNet to a ConvNeXt which are responsible for this. On the other end of the spectrum we examine the ViT, as a non-convolutional architecture using attention and with an isotropic design after the PatchStem, see Fig. 2. As an intermediate architecture we study the isotropic ConvNeXt which shares the large PatchStem $(16 \times 16)$ and the isotropic structure with ViT but still uses convolutions instead of attention. By examining two extremes and an intermediate case, our analysis covers a large spectrum of existing architecture components. Table 1 shows the results of all architectures in this basic training setting. We report clean accuracy achieved by standard training, and clean and robust accuracy (in the various threat models) of the classifier obtained with $\ell_{\infty}$ -adversarial training. The number of parameters and FLOPs show that the compared models have similar capacity. From ResNet to ConvNeXt. We notice in Table 1 that the ResNet-50 with $\ell_{\infty}$ -adversarial training shows little robustness to unseen attacks $(\ell_2, \ell_1)$ . At the same time ConvNeXt T, the "modernized" version of ResNets, improves robust accuracy w.r.t. $\ell_{\infty}$ $(+6.2\%)$ , but the largest gains are attained in $\ell_{2}$ - $16.1\%$ vs $42.5\%$ and $\ell_{1}$ -robustness $(2.5\%$ vs $15.6\%)$ . Two key differences of ConvNext and ResNet are the PatchStem, see Fig. 2, and depthwise convolutions. The PatchStem is an aggressive form of dimensionality reduction and low dimension is in particular helpful for $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ -robustness. On the other hand depthwise convolution plus the following $1\times 1$ -convolution can be seen as low-rank decomposition of a standard convolution which severely limits the flexibility of the model. Just these two changes of a ResNet-50 improve $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness and almost close the gap to a ConvNeXt regarding generalization to $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ . From ConvNeXt to ViT. While some of the novel components of ConvNeXts are inspired by the Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021), they preserve the typical structure of ResNets, that is progressive downsampling and convolutional layers. However, Liu et al. (2022) further introduce Isotropic ConvNeXt, which creates tokens similarly to ViTs, and these are then processed by a sequence of identical residual blocks (with no downsampling, hence the name isotropic) as in ViTs, until a final linear classifier. The blocks of a ViT rely on multi-head self-attention layers (Vaswani et al., 2017), while Isotropic ConvNeXt replaces them with depthwise convolutions. It can be thus considered an intermediate step between ConvNeXt and ViT. Using only 50 epochs of adversarial training together with a weak initialization and augmentation, the ViT-S performs significantly worse than ConvNeXt and Isotropic ConvNeXt in $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness, although it shows good generalization especially to $\ell_1$ . In the following we show how it is possible to improve the performance of the isotropic architectures (Isotropic ConvNeXt and ViT) with a convolutional stem. # 3.3. Convolutional Stem Xiao et al. (2021) propose to replace the patch embedder in ViTs with a convolutional block (ConvStem) consisting of several convolutional layers alternating with normalization and activation layers. While the PatchStem in ViTs divides the input in disjoint patches and creates tokens from them, the ConvStem progressively downsamples the input image until it has the right resolution to be fed to the transformer blocks. Xiao et al. (2021) show that this results in more stable training which is robust to the choice of optimizer and hyperparameters. As adversarial training is more difficult than standard training, we check if adding a ConvStem has a similar positive effect. As both ViTs and Isotropic ConvNeXts divide the input image into $16 \times 16$ patches, we use for both the convolutional stem of Xiao et al. (2021), which has four convolutional layers with stride 2 each followed by layer normalization and GELU activation. Since ConvNeXt uses a PatchStem with $4 \times 4$ -patches, the ConvStem of ViTs ![](images/b6577d964ea232bcb3889a832499f11f40ee17aeea06d02b62a1b043d5363e67.jpg) Figure 2. Convolutional stem for ConvNeXt. We use two convolution layers each followed by LayerNorm and GELU to replace the 4x4 patch of the standard ConvNeXt model (PatchStem). ![](images/757b804661a0789fd910c758212782c7eaed84e75d2389f34a2fd8128f6e5d36.jpg) would not work. Therefore we design a specific convolutional stem with only two convolutional layers with kernel size 3 and stride 2, see Fig. 2. Adding a ConvStem has only minimal impact on the number of parameters and FLOPs of the models (see Table 1), especially for ConvNeXt. More details on the convolutional stem design and ablation studies on its effect on unseen threat models can be found in App. B. In Table 1 we show the effect of using a convolutional stem for the three architectures: for both isotropic architectures it notably improves the results of standard pre-training as well as robustness (and its generalization) for adversarially trained models. In particular, Isotropic ConvNeXt + ConvStem achieves the highest robust accuracy in $\ell_2$ and $\ell_1$ . For the ConvNeXt, which even in its original form performs well, the convolutional stem has mixed impact on the robustness, possibly because the clean model used for initialization is worse. When using strong pre-training and heavy augmentation the ConvStem leads even for the ConvNeXt to consistent gains in $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness as well as $\ell_1 / \ell_2$ , see Table 2. Our results in this basic training setup show that the ConvStem is a simple and effective architecture modification which has significant impact on robustness. In the following, we further analyze the interplay of architecture and various choices in adversarial training. # 4. Effect of Strong Pre-Training and Heavy Data Augmentation on Robustness We now move on to study how to exploit two established techniques for adversarial robustness, leading to an advanced training setting on ImageNet using strong pretraining and heavy data augmentation. Adversarial training is done as in the previous section now starting from a setting with basic augmentation and random initialization, which is progressively updated with the changes detailed in Table 2 # 4.1. trained on ImageNet-21k or JFT achieve significantly higher accuracy on ImageNet-1k than those trained on ImageNet-1k from random initialization (Wightman, 2019). Hendrycks et al. (2019) suggested that the same holds for adversarial training. However, our goal is not to use a larger training set but rather better exploit ImageNet-1k. As adversarial training on ImageNet is a non-trivial optimization problem, where runs can also fail completely, see Debenedetti et al. (2023), we propose to initialize adversarial training from a fully trained (on ImageNet-1k) standard model. Although the clean model is clearly not adversariably robust, starting from a point with low clean loss helps considerably in the first stages of training. Short fine-tuning of clean models to become adversarily robust has been discussed in (Jeddi et al., 2020; Croce & Hein, 2022) but without achieving robustness comparable to full adversarial training. In the following we use as initialization the standard models available in the timm library or from the original papers. For the models with convolutional stem no such models are available. For these we randomly initialize the ConvStem and the remaining layers with the weights of the corresponding non-ConvStem models, followed by standard training for 100 epochs to reach good clean accuracy (see more details and the performance of these classifiers in App. B.4). Interestingly, just changing from our weak initialization of the previous section with only 100 epochs of pre-training with basic augmentation to strongly pre-trained models has a huge effect on clean as well as $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy, across architectures, see Table 2. Notably, the effects on the isotropic architectures, which are known to be harder to train, are even higher than for the ConvNeXt. Even at this stage the ViT-S + ConvStem has already $2.5\%$ better $l_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy (44.3% vs 41.8%) than the XCiT-S model of Debenedetti et al. (2023). # 4.2. Heavy Data Augmentation The second aspect we analyze is how to take advantage of heavy augmentation techniques like RandAugment (Cubuk et al., 2020), MixUp (Zhang et al., 2018) and CutMix (Yun et al., 2019), which are crucial for the performance of standard models, in adversarial training. In particular, Bai et al. (2021) note that for ViTs combining such heavy data augmentation with adversarial training makes the models collapse, and thus design a schedule to progressively increase the augmentation intensity. Similarly, Debenedetti et al. (2023) report better performance for robust ViTs when only weak augmentations (random crop, horizontal flip, color jitter) are used, and that ConvNeXt training even diverges if heavy augmentations are not excluded. Instead we show that initializing adversarial training with a well-trained standard classifier makes it possible to use heavy augmentation techniques from the beginning, and benefit from them, even for small models and shorter training schedules. In contrast, training a ConvNeXt with heavy augmentations and random initialization failed. As heavy augmentations we use RandAugment, CutMix, MixUp, Random Erasing (Zhong et al., 2020) (with hyperparameters similar to Liu et al. (2022), see App. A). We also use Exponential Moving Average (EMA) with a decay of 0.9999 and label smoothing with parameter 0.1 for consistency with Liu et al. (2022). However, we observe little to no effect of EMA on robustness. In Table 2 one can see that adding heavy data augmentation on top of strong pre-training significantly boosts the performance of the ConvNeXts in clean and $\ell_{\infty}$ robust accuracy. Interestingly, only the ConvNeXt + ConvStem has further strong improvements in the unseen $\ell_{2}$ and $\ell_{1}$ -threat models. For the isotropic architectures, heavy augmentations have marginal effect on $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness, although improve robustness to unseen attacks. Isotropic architectures require longer training to benefit from heavy augmentations. We highlight that at this point our ConvNeXt-T and ConvNeXt-T + ConvStem already have higher (+2.1% and +3.1% respectively) robustness w.r.t. $\ell_{\infty}$ than the ConvNeXt-T from Debenedetti et al. (2023), and similarly our ViT-S + ConvStem and Isotropic ConvNeXt + ConvStem outperform XCiT-S (Debenedetti et al., 2023) (detailed comparison to # SOTA in Table 3). Longer training. Adding heavy data augmentation increases the complexity of the learning problem, which requires longer training, in particular for isotropic architectures. Thus we extend the training time from 50 to 300 epochs. As expected we see the strongest improvements for the isotropic architectures but even for ConvNeXt one observes consistent gains. The ConvNeXt-T + ConvStem, with $49.5\%$ robust accuracy, outperforms all classifiers reported in Debenedetti et al. (2023) and Peng et al. (2023), including those with up to 4 times more parameters. # 5. Comparison with SOTA Models In Table 3 we compare our classifiers with models from prior works trained for adversarial robustness w.r.t. $\ell_{\infty}$ at $\epsilon_{\infty} = 4 / 255$ on ImageNet. For each model we report number of parameters and FLOPs, the number of training epochs, the number of steps in the inner maximization, and clean and robust accuracy (AutoAttack on RobustBench validation set) in the three threat models. We group the models according to size for fair comparison, distinguishing small (<30M parameters), medium ( $\approx$ 50M params) and large models ( $\geq$ 80M params). 1-Step vs 2-Step Adversarial Training. Current works use one to three steps of PGD to solve the inner problem, see column "Adv. Steps" in Table 3. It is an important question if our gains, e.g. compared to works like Debenedetti et al. (2023) who use a single step, are just a result of the stronger attack at training time. We test this by training a ConvNeXt + ConvStem model with strong pre-training and heavy augmentation with 1-step APGD adversarial training for 50 epochs. We get a $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy of $46.4\%$ (clean acc. is $71.0\%$ ) compared to $47.5\%$ with 2-step APGD which is just a difference of $1.1\%$ . Thus our gains are only marginally influenced by stronger adversarial training. Moreover, our ConvNeXt + ConvStem models with 50 epochs of adversarial training outperform all existing SOTA models even though the computational cost of training them is lower (50 epochs of 2-step AT correspond roughly to 75 epochs of 1-step AT and 37.5 epochs of 3-step AT). Scaling to larger models. We apply our training scheme introduced in the previous sections to architectures with significantly more parameters and FLOPs. We focus on ConvNeXt-S/B and ViT-M/B1: in particular, for ConvNeXt-B we adapt the convolutional stem used for ConvNeXt-T by adding an extra convolutional layer, while for the ViTs we just adjust the number of output channels to match the feature dimension of the transformer blocks (more details in App. B). Among small models, all three architectures equipped with ConvStem outperform in terms of $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness all competitors of similar size with up to $5.1\%$ improvement upon the ConvNeXt-T of Debenedetti et al. (2023). Moreover, our ConvNeXt-T + ConvStem is with $49.5\%$ robust accuracy $0.6\%$ better than the RobArch-L (Peng et al., 2023) (the previously second most robust model) which has $3.6\times$ more parameters and FLOPs. The ConvStem positively impacts generalization of robustness to unseen attacks of all three architectures, with improvements between $2.2\%$ and $4.2\%$ for $\ell_{2}$ and $1.8\%$ and $5.2\%$ for $\ell_{1}$ (with respect to the XCiT-S12). For medium models the picture is the same, our ViT-M + ConvStem and the ConvNeXt-S + ConvStem outperform in seen and unseen threat models the XCiT-M12. For large models we compare to the previously most robust model, the ViT-B of Rebuffi et al. (2022), with $53.5\%$ $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy (the model is not available so we cannot evaluate $\ell_{1}$ - and $\ell_{2}$ -robustness). It is remarkable that our ConvNeXt-B + ConvStem with only 50 epochs of training outperforms this ViT-B trained for 300 epochs already by $0.9\%$ and with 250 epochs training even by $2.5\%$ . Influence of Resolution and Fine-Tuning In the following we analyze how robustness behaves under changes of test time resolution, and robust fine-tuning to either a larger radius on ImageNet or other datasets. Improving robustness via increasing test-time image resolution. Unlike small datasets like CIFAR-10, for ImageNet the input images are resized before inference. Using higher resolution at test time can lead to improved clean accuracy for standard ImageNet models (Touvron et al., 2019; El-Nouby et al., 2021). On the other hand increasing dimension for fixed radius makes the $\ell_{\infty}$ -threat model more powerful. To study which effect prevails, we test clean and $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy for each of our models from 'small' (300 epochs) and 'large' (250 epochs) in Table 3 when varying test time input resolution between 192 and 384. Note that all models have been trained on $224 \times 224$ images only, and no fine-tuning to different resolutions is done: for ViTs we have to adapt the models via interpolation of the positional embedding as suggested by Caron et al. (2021). Fig. 3 shows that all classifiers obtain highest robustness for image resolutions 256 or 288, higher than the training one. For faster evaluation we use for this plot $\mathrm{APGD}_{\mathrm{T - DLR}}$ with 40 iterations and 3 target classes. Then, we select for each model the best input resolution, and evaluate $\ell_{\infty}$ -robustness with AutoAttack in Table 4. Increasing input resolution significantly improves clean and $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy. Our ConvNeXt-B + ConvStem attains SOTA $76.9\%$ and $57.3\%$ clean and robust accuracy, respectively, at resolution 256. Additional results on the role of the input resolution can be found in App. C.3, including a discussion of what it means for threat models other than $\ell_{\infty}$ . Fine-tuning to larger radius. While $\epsilon = 4 / 255$ is the standard radius for the $\ell_{\infty}$ -threat model on ImageNet, even larger perturbations might still be imperceptible. Debenedetti et al. (2023) train XCiTs with $\epsilon = 8 / 255$ from scratch for 110 epochs. However, given the success of using a warm start for adversarial training (see Sec. 4.1), we propose to fine-tune the model fully trained for robustness at $\epsilon = 4 / 255$ with adversarial training with the larger radius. Such classifiers already have non-trivial robustness at $\epsilon = 8 / 255$ , and we expect they require only relatively small changes to adapt to the larger radius. We use our models from Table 3 to fine-tune for 25 epochs (details in App. A.5), and report the results in Table 5: our ConvNeXt-B + ConvStem improves significantly over the previous best result both in terms of clean and robust accuracy, even though we just use relatively short fine-tuning. Fine-tuning to other datasets. We fine-tune our models trained to be robust at radius 8/255 from Table 5 to other datasets and compare to the results of Debenedetti et al. (2023) in Table 6. For Flowers-102 (resolution $224 \times 224$ ) the improvement over XCiT in robust accuracy is similar to the difference of the models in Table 5 and shows that the benefits of more robust models transfers to smaller datasets. For CIFAR (resolution $32 \times 32$ ) our models tend to achieve similar robustness as the XCiT models but at a much better clean accuracy. We expect that here even stronger robustness gains are feasible by optimized fine-tuning. For details on the fine-tuning, see App. C.4. # 7. Conclusion We have examined two extreme representatives of todays modern architectures, ViT and ConvNeXt, regarding adversarial robustness. We have shown that ConvNeXt + ConvStem yields SOTA $\ell_{\infty}$ -robust accuracy as well as good generalization to unseen threat models such as $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ across a range of parameters and FLOPs. Given that for smaller model sizes the ConvNeXt + ConvStem is much easier to train than the ViT, it has the potential to become similarly popular for studying adversarial robustness on ImageNet than (Wide)-ResNets for CIFAR-10. On the other hand ViT + ConvStem excels in generalization to unseen threat models. Thus there is no clear winner between ViT and ConvNeXt but we think that the findings of this paper open up a number of interesting future research directions. # Acknowledgements The authors acknowledge support from the DFG Cluster of Excellence "Machine Learning - New Perspectives for Science", EXC 2064/1, project number 390727645. # References Andriushchenko, M., Croce, F., Flammarion, N., and Hein, M.
